children: By Reshma Kapadia and George Glover

Supporters of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva were celebrating on Monday following Brazil's shock election result, but Brazilian stocks plummeted on the leftist incumbent's narrow victory. The sharp selloff could pave the way for a buying opportunity.

The iShares MSCI Brazil exchange-traded fund fell 24% in morning trading after Lula won a fourth term in an upset win over right-wing Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, reversing the gains that were logged after October's first-round election suggested that Bolsonaro was the favorite for Sunday's runoff election. It was the first time since 1989 that a first-round winner hasn't gone on to win the runoff.

The market's initial move stems from concerns about Brazil's worsening finances and worries that Lula would be less likely than Bolsonaro to implement the fiscal discipline needed to stave off a fiscal crisis. Both candidates had offered populist measures into the election to offset the impact of high interest rates on households.

Volatility could continue, with Bolsonaro looking to annul the results even as some of his allies have accepted them. But the selloff could eventually create opportunity for investors, who note that Lula's last term didn't produce as dramatic shifts in fiscal policy that bears had initially worried about. And this time he is even more constrained.

"Markets are clearly panic selling and Brazilian assets already looked reasonably valued versus global peers so this will take us back to quite attractive returns with the caveat that volatility is clearly likely in the short term," says Leon Eidelman, a manager on several emerging markets strategies, including the JP Morgan Active Developing Markets Equity ETF. "Is the current scenario any different to what we had six months ago? Seems unclear to me that it is."

That's not to undersell Brazil's fiscal problems. Brazil's gross government debt is about 83% of gross domestic product, the highest in 20 years outside of Covid and with much of the debt tied to mandatory spending. Interest rates of 13.75% makes that debt even more painful. Lula will start his fourth term with debt on the rise, and his campaign vows to ease the sting of higher rates with greater social benefits will only add to the dismal outlook for the country's finances.

But Congress will likely block a sharp move to the left, as Lula faces the most conservative Congress since the country's return to democracy in 1985. The right will hold about 59% of seats in the Chamber of Deputies and almost two-thirds in the Senate. Bolsonaro's Liberal Party is the biggest force in the lower house.

"Bolsonaro was expected to impose fiscal discipline from the presidency, but Lula may find that Congress and the bond markets impose it on him instead," says Gavekal analyst Rohan Daswani in a note to clients.
Stepping back from the politics is the geopolitics. Brazil has emerged as a critical supplier to the global economy and is well-positioned amid the growing rivalry between the U.S. and China.

The U.S. is looking to forge closer ties with Brazil to access its critical minerals and for defense, energy, and data center-oriented deals. Meanwhile, China is a big customer for its raw materials, commodities, and agriculture. Despite the loss by Bolsonaro, a Trump ally, Brazil will be too important for the U.S. to ignore if it wants to diversify its supply chains away from China, Daswani adds. Earlier this year, USA Rare Earth agreed to buy Serra Verde Group for $2.8 billion.

Bargain-hunters may wait to jump into Brazil's markets until they get indications of who Lula picks as finance minister and what his fiscal agenda might look like. If he opts for Vice-President Geraldo Alckmin or Banco Central President Gabriel Galípolo as finance minister, TS Lombard analyst Elizabeth Johnson says it could help rebuild market confidence.

It would also be helpful if Lula can show he is willing to cut some mandatory spending before the 2027 budget is passed and that he is finally willing to put Brazil back on a more fiscally sustainable path to avert a fiscal crisis next year.

But expectations are very low, cautions Thea Jamison, manager at Change Global Investments, so anything even marginally positive in terms of cabinet appointments, spending restraint, or debt stabilization could be positive. She notes that exporters could do well as they benefit from a weaker real and continued strength in commodities.
